verification.note: Complete publisher preface vii–xvi/all17notes, imprint, contents and acknowledgments xvii freshly read in the original Cambridge frontmatter PDF. Butterfield/Laslett viii, Bailyn/Robbins ix, Oakeshott x/xiii, qualified Kuhn xi–xiii and Skinner xiv checked. Retrospective narrative and later reported Kuhn agreement remain attributed. sources.title: Samuel James, J. G. A. Pocock and the Idea of the Cambridge School (accepted manuscript).
sources.citation: Samuel James, “J. G. A. Pocock and the Idea of the ‘Cambridge School’ in the History of Political Thought,” History of European Ideas45(1),2019, DOI firstposted2018; accepted manuscript in Cambridge repository, selected sections I–II and IV–V, no stable print pagination.

verification.note: Accepted DOCX manuscript freshly retrieved from Cambridge institutional repository, main body and footnotes extracted separately. Selected opening I and II, IV Oakeshott discussion and complete V/conclusion/acknowledgments read; no print-page equivalence asserted. James challenges the conventional early Laslett/linguistic-philosophy formation narrative and foregrounds Butterfield, historiography and Oakeshott. This is a named scholar’s critical reconstruction, not new reading of private correspondence or all Pocock originals. James’s2013interview with Pocock acknowledged by the author, not newly read. Held-only reception source; no James full node.

gm163_robertson_pocock_2025.note: Fresh original publisher PDF from the author’s Cambridge repository read at1–4, with cover identifying23April2025online release. Robertson’s emphasis on historiography, his distinction between changing projects and his response to Pocock’s own complaints remain his interpretation. Quoted1952thesis passage is mediated through Robertson2; thesis, private correspondence and late political essays not newly read. Full later article sections and notes not read in this continuation.
